title: The Jam-Smudged Letter
markdown:
St. Cuthbert's Abbey smelled of beeswax and pickled walnuts, a pairing no liturgy had requested. Scholarship was prized, especially the sort that photographed well at the benefactors' tea. Patronage was discussed with more heat than salvation. Piety, when it appeared, liked a window seat.

Sister Dara Quinn did not boom in the cloisters. Her mind, however, kept a hidden garden of solutions. She could untangle wool as if it had asked her politely, and she could lift a cipher faster than a hare leaves a meadow. The same mind lived in a woman who dreaded the weekly address. Before a crowd her voice shrank to leaf-rustle. The fear stuck like moss.

Bishop Vale presided over the earthly side of holiness. He was a man of girth and of the opinion that abbey ledgers existed to impress the wealthy. He polished a gilded chalice and, with the same cloth, his reputation. Prayers came with dedications suitable for donors. A compliment, he believed, outranked a dozen whispered psalms. Fine vestments outranked patched ones. After each pronouncement he adjusted his starched collar, as if the collar had done the theology.

One autumn morning, leaves the color of a robin's breast and the air promising woodsmoke, a stable boy arrived breathless and berry-smudged. The letter he carried was sealed not with the abbey's dignified wax but with what was, on close inspection and a cautious sniff, strawberry jam. The script inside ran sharp and urgent, lines tilting as if the writer had been interrupted by a kitchen. It was meant to confirm a donation from the Fitzwilliam Puddleton clan—a name as long as a winter night—for the infirmary that mended bones and issued broth when fevers made a bed feel like a boat. Bishop Vale read, deflated like a bellows, and went the color of an overripe plum.

"A jammed seal. Strange scribbles. Undignified. Who can say what dire pronouncements lurk under this confectionary catastrophe?" His complaints about decorum filled the scriptorium. The precious gift seemed to be sliding off the table like mist.

The assembly was called in haste. The grand hall, usually the murmur of prayer and the rustle of parchment, filled with nervous chatter. Vale smoothed robes that were already smooth, adjusted his pectoral cross, and addressed a culinary coded crisis at a volume that suggested panic had found a pulpit. Elder sisters exchanged glances and tightened rosaries. Younger brothers wrung their hands until the knuckles shone. No one wished to be the person who lost blankets because of jam.

Dara stood. Her heart knocked against her ribs. Knuckles whitened on worn beads. "Perhaps I might have a look. At the letter."

A hush fell that was almost a third presence. Eyes turned—from abbess to newest novice—to the nun who usually vanished into tapestry, her presence as slight as a moth. Vale, relieved to pass a problem, put the sticky page into her trembling hands. "See to it, Sister. Publicly. We cannot have a riddle of preserves undermining charity and tarnishing St. Cuthbert's."

This was the hour she had rehearsed in dread: the hall, the sea of faces, the trapped-bird breath. The jam, ridiculous and earthly, sat on the paper like a dare. She thought of the infirmary cots, of quiet suffering that did not care about pulpit volume, and took the spring breath she needed. She unfurled the letter.

Diagonal lines. Unusual curves. A simple substitution, the sort used by novices passing notes, made unnecessarily hard by a smear that hid one crucial character—an S, or a G, under a glistening seed. She sounded the alphabet against the shapes until the hidden letter gave. She began to read, and the stream found its bed. Her voice, at first a whisper, grew steadier with each clause.

"To the esteemed Abbey of St. Cuthbert. We, the family of Lord Fitzwilliam Puddleton the Third, send greetings and our sincerest apologies. Our youngest son, Bartholomew, in youthful exuberance, mistook the message meant for you for a recipe for his grandmother's famous jam tarts. He has jammed our correspondence and heartily apologizes for the sticky situation. We enclose the true intended message, detailing our donation for the infirmary, with regrets for Bartholomew's culinary enthusiasm." She allowed the smallest smile. "He prefers the art of baking to diplomatic pledges."

Laughter started as hesitant titter and became a hall's worth of relief, sugar going into tea. Vale clutched his chest as if revelation had been slightly silly. "Jam tarts? The very Bartholomew who once offered a pouch of shiny pebbles and an enthusiastic badger in payment for a new gargoyle?"

The coil in the room went slack. Dara had not once dropped a word. Her voice had not been a cathedral bell. It had been heard, clear enough to carry to the door.

The donation stood. The infirmary would have blankets and balms enough for the winter. Bartholomew Fitzwilliam Puddleton was advised, with amusement, to keep his talents in kitchens and well away from seals and official ink. Dara returned to puzzles and old texts, which still suited her better than a dais. The moss-fear had thinned, a sapling through hard ground. In the corridor after, a novice asked her to look at another muddled note from a farmer who wrote as if startled, and she said yes without first consulting the nearest shadow.
characters: Dara Quinn (code-breaking nun), Bishop Vale (donor strategist)
